steps.say: A frozen model, and a memory bolted on beside it.
Past turns go in on the right as a few final-layer states, and come back out as keys and values for every attention layer.

scenes.headline: MemOnce: write once, retrieve once, decode per layer
scenes.sub: What it keeps, what it reads, and what the multipliers compare
scenes.say: I'm Engram. Let's follow one conversation into MemOnce's memory and one question back out.

heads: Each turn keeps only its tail
The newest blocks are always read
The question scores every older block, once
The same blocks feed every attention layer
params.question: question key
params.tail: the last 64 states of each turn

steps.say: Each turn runs through the model once. Only the final-layer states of its last 64 tokens are kept. The rest is thrown away.
The newest 16 blocks stay on the GPU as a short window, read on every question.
A question gets one key. One cosine pass over the older blocks picks the top 64. That choice is made once, before any token is generated.
Each attention layer decodes the same blocks into its own keys and values. A block that missed the cut is invisible to all of them.

scenes.title: What full attention keeps
scenes.text: 8 layers x 2 x 1024 x 2 bytes = 32 KiB

parts.note: only every fourth layer is attention
parts.say: Qwen three point five, four B, has eight attention layers.

parts.note: a key and a value, 1,024 numbers each
parts.say: Each keeps a key and a value per token.

parts.note: per token; a million tokens is 32 GiB
parts.say: Thirty-two kibibytes a token. A million tokens is thirty-two gibibytes.

left.title: The paper's 1,313x
left.say: The headline divides thirty-two gigabytes of full cache by twenty-five megabytes of states, before they are decoded.

right.title: What the GPU holds
right.say: Decoded for eight layers, those states are a hundred and sixty mebibytes. Still flat at any length. And the whole stored pool is fifty-one times smaller than full KV.

steps.say: Reading everything is quadratic in the attention layers. About two hundred eighty-seven seconds at a million tokens.
MemOnce writes in short segments: forty-one seconds. That is the six point nine.
But look at the short end. At thirty-two thousand tokens MemOnce is slower.

scenes.title: On an RTX 3090, 132,310 tokens
scenes.note: Synthetic history; decoded KV measured 160.00 MiB
scenes.say: I ran the released checkpoint on a 3090. At a hundred and thirty-two thousand tokens, writing took about half the time of a full prefill, and the decoded cache measured exactly a hundred and sixty mebibytes.

steps.say: The memory benchmarks. I recomputed every MemOnce column from the released result files, and they match.
steps.caption: MemOnce 4B: 60.07 against 54.30

steps.say: It wins most where reading everything drowns. On LoCoMo, full context still wins.

scenes.title: What it gives up
scenes.say: The price: a turn survives only as its tail, and retrieval happens once. In my needle test the right block was retrieved, and the answer was still wrong once in three.

scenes.text: Store 640 bytes a token, attend over a fixed 160 MiB, and bet everything on one retrieval.
scenes.say: Store six hundred forty bytes a token, attend over a fixed hundred and sixty mebibytes, and bet everything on one retrieval.
MemOnce: write once, retrieve once, decode for every layer.
